description_full: Western Digital Corporation engages in the development, manufacture, and sale of data storage devices and solutions based on hard disk drive (HDD) technology in the United States, Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. The company offers internal HDDs, data center drives, data center platforms, external drives, portable drives, NAS for home and office, and accessories. It sells its data storage devices and solutions through its computer sales personnel, dealers, distributors, retailers, and subsidiaries. The company has a collaboration with Open Quantum Design for the development of quantum error correction technology and related systems to advance reliable quantum computing. Western Digital Corporation was founded in 1970 and is headquartered in San Jose, California.

Each employee generates $88K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $5K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 14× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: Western Digital Corporation is a large-cap technology business with a $110.7B market cap on $12.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and -0% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 12% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 28%.

The business throws off $3.5B in free cash flow — roughly 27 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.42×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
Accruals are elevated at +39.6% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 27× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 34% operating margin runs 28pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.47x).
It accounts for 0.3% of sector revenue and 0.4% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+8.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 143% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 36% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 63% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 83% and a beta of 1.50, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 3.05 vs 5y 1.92), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $2.9B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 59% in the 2020 crash, 55% in the 2022 bear market and 75% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $210 (margin of safety -41%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 87%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $123 to $360 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 10.4 vs 27.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 23% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 24 covering analysts target $613 on average, 107% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 10% falls short of the cost of capital of 11.8%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.09).
It runs a 28% gross margin and converts 27% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 7/9, but cash conversion of only 0.42x and high accruals (+39.6% of assets).
ROE of 106% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.6x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 25pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 9.0% of revenue on R&D and 1.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $527.0M (0% of market cap).
Warning signs: a Beneish M-score that flags possible earnings manipulation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.6% over 3 years, -5.3% over 5 years and -0.1% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 21%).
At current returns, reinvesting 24% of profits supports about 2.4% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 36.1% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00 and a backlog worth 0% of annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 3.2% of sales), a maintenance pace.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 90%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (22 sales, net $6.5M sold).
It returns 2.5% a year to shareholders (2.3% in buybacks and 0.2% in dividends).
The share count has grown 3.6% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 40,000 employees, each generates about $323K of revenue, in line with the Technology median.
That works out to $88K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.5M (14x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
